Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: Learn basic course management, recognise the distances and danger that matter, and build the habit of choosing a sensible target before every shot. Try ideas here, see the range of possible results, and learn why a choice helps. We score your decision, not one lucky ball. Start with three choices on the same hole.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: This flag is tucked close to the edge of the green. Tap the highlighted target to aim directly at it, then reveal the shots. Your best shot may be close, but your normal misses need room too.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: Now aim at the far-left part of the green, away from the water. Moving this far gives up closeness to the flag and brings the left-side misses into play. More caution is not automatically a better decision.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: Try the highlighted target toward the roomy part of the green. You give up a little closeness to the flag to make room for your misses. This is the best sampled target in our model: a sensible blend of opportunity and safety, not a guarantee.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: Carry is how far you intend the ball to travel before landing. It is a useful starting point for course management because rollout depends heavily on the ground. Wind and imperfect contact can still change actual carry. In practice, set direction on the course and distance with the Intended carry bar below the course, or on the right in full screen.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: The app simulates 4,000 possible shots from your selected profile. Together they show a range of outcomes, rather than one guaranteed average shot. In normal practice, the outline shows the main carry pattern and the dots show final positions after rollout. Some misses fall outside the outline.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: We judge your target choice, rather than one lucky or unlucky ball. Too aggressive brings costly trouble into play. Too conservative makes the next shot unnecessarily hard. Look for a balance between danger and useful distance. The blue comparison in practice is the best sampled alternative.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions
entries.text: The shot-selection view stays clear of extra predictions. Use the distances, visible hazards and conditions, just as you would on a real course. Choose your target before seeing its pattern. Then adjust and compare to test your ideas using the same misses.

entries.section: Introduction — purpose, slides and illustration captions

entries.text: Learn the basics, recognise what matters, and practise choosing a sensible target before every shot. This app trains your eyes and judgement through experience. Try a five-shot learning round, or explore the lessons for more guided examples.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Give costly misses more room. Avoiding every possible miss is not the goal.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples

entries.text: Aim beyond the front water so shorter finishes have more room. You accept a longer putt to reduce penalty risk.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: OB: play again from where you were

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: The thick red lines highlight the OB boundary. On a real course, OB is normally marked by white stakes or lines. If your ball goes beyond the boundary, the shot counts, you add one penalty stroke, and you play again from your previous spot. Here you started on the tee, so your next tee shot is your third shot.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Water: a penalty and a drop

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: The blue outline marks the water. Taking penalty relief adds one stroke, then you play from a drop. The drop is based on where the ball last crossed the penalty-area edge; red and yellow markings give different options. This picture shows our example’s designated drop.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: The gold outline marks the bunker. There is no automatic penalty stroke for landing in it. Think of sand as extra work on your next shot. Our Tour-player reference puts a 20 yd bunker shot about {value 1} strokes harder than the same distance from fairway; at 60 yd, about {value 2}. These are averages, not penalties or your personal score.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Thicker grass can make clean contact harder. Trees can block the direct route, so you may need to play a recovery shot back into space. Neither adds an automatic penalty just for landing there, but getting back on track can cost strokes.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Make room for the costly miss

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Gold shows the spread when you aim directly at the flag. Some shorter misses reach the front water. Blue shows the recommended target farther beyond the flag: it gives those misses more room. Each outline contains about 80% of the modeled shots. Water percentages also count misses outside it. A safer target can still have a few costly misses. Next, try that target.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Move the pattern away from the costly side.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Choose room for your misses, not just a line for your best shot.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Move toward the safer part of the green, away from the side pond. Your misses need room too.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Aim the whole spread, not just one ball

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Gold is centered on the flag; blue is centered on the recommended target farther from the side pond. These spreads use this lesson’s fixed player profile. Notice how moving the center gives ordinary misses more room. The blue target reduces water risk rather than guaranteeing every shot stays dry.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Move your aim when one side is costly

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Imagine a dartboard. On a clear board, you aim at the bullseye. Now imagine a friend’s hand covers the right edge. You would shift your aim left: you can still hit the board, while giving a small miss more room before it reaches their hand. Water beside a green creates the same target decision. The hand represents the danger beside the green.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Understand when laying back is worthwhile.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Compare the cost of the longer next shot with the risk the longer club adds.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: The shorter shot finds the widest, safest part of the fairway, but leaves a longer approach. Here the longer target is worth a little more trouble because it leaves you much closer to the green.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Laying back has a distance cost

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: From 100 yd in the fairway, our historical PGA TOUR reference averages {value 1} strokes to finish the hole. From 150 yd, it averages {value 2}. That is about {value 3} extra strokes per shot, or {value 4} per 100 similar shots. These totals include the approach, short game and putting. A layup that leaves 150 instead of 100 must save enough trouble to justify that added distance cost. This is a Tour average, not a minimum cost or your personal prediction.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Not every extra 50 yards costs the same

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Compare the fairway reference: 50→100 yd adds {value 1} strokes; 100→150 adds {value 2}; 150→200 adds {value 3}. The first two are almost the same here. The bigger jump appears farther out, where you typically need a longer club. So do not assume every layup is cheap—or every extra yard is worth the risk. In the guided hole, both targets are reachable: the safer 190 yd shot gives up useful distance, and the longer target wins overall in this model.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Find a useful target beyond the flag.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: The flag is a destination for the ball, not automatically the best target for the full pattern.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Give the bunker beside this pin more room by moving toward the wider part of the green.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Dispersion means the area your shots spread across. Longer shots usually have a wider spread. Picture a flashlight: nearby it makes a small spot; farther away the spot gets wider. A wedge can often aim closer to the flag. A long iron usually needs more room for misses.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Let the club change your target

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Here the flag is tucked near the right edge and a bunker. A wedge’s smaller spread can fit around a tighter target near the flag. A long iron’s wider spread needs its center farther toward the middle of the green. That may mean a longer putt, but fewer misses into the difficult side. Both pictures use the same green; their spreads and targets illustrate the idea, not a scored recommendation.

entries.section: Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
Lessons — all lesson explanations and examples
entries.text: Short-sided means you missed the green on the side where the flag is close to the edge. You have little green between your ball and the hole, so stopping a chip can be difficult—especially across a bunker. The fat side is the side with more green to work with. Giving your spread room toward that side can leave an easier recovery. It means room around the flag, not simply a shot that finishes short of the green. More room helps; the lie and other hazards still matter.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Basic training uses a straight, centered Gaussian shot pattern. Handicap sets an illustrative training bag: driver total-distance limits are 280 yd (scratch), 265 yd (5), 250 yd (10), and 225 yd (20). These are profile limits, not measured averages or universal personal maximums. Approach shots allow up to the profile’s 3 wood. Left/right comes from the main view; the depth bar changes depth along that aim line. The target specifies intended carry. After you choose a target, a short line and hollow finish marker show planned straight-line rollout before curve or random misses. Zoom in for a closer view. This planning aid does not reveal dispersion or the recommended target. After a normal practice shot, white markers show the core center flight landing and finish; water contact stops its rollout. Zero-roll shots use one location. The shortest estimated club that can carry that distance is selected, then club-specific rollout determines its planned finish. Core σ scales by intended carry divided by that club’s stock carry capacity. The table below shows the current profile’s full-swing assumptions. These are illustrative presets, not measured handicap averages. Member preview uses your saved club distances, shapes and miss settings. The shortest club that can carry to the target is selected automatically. Core σ, curve, usual bias and big-miss offsets scale by intended carry / stock carry, with a 25% floor; start angle, height and big-miss probability stay fixed. Driver is excluded for approaches; stock distance uses saved carry, with zero rollout. Custom curve and bias may move the mean finish away from the nominal target. Club carry accepts 50–330 yd and rollout 0–40 yd.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: 80% of core shots lie within ±1.282σ on each individual axis; a joint 80% ellipse is larger (radius 1.794σ). The core contour is shown only after you commit. The blue comparison uses the same player and club-selection rules at the best sampled aim. Member big misses use a mixture component with twice the core σ plus the configured directional shift and carry loss.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Next-shot costs use Mark Broadie’s historical PGA TOUR benchmark (2003–2010), with separate distance curves for fairway, rough, sand, recovery and putting. A 150 yd fairway shot has a 2.945-stroke reference; sand at 20 yd has 2.53, versus 2.82 at 40 yd. These are reference-player values, not your personal expected score. Handicap changes your simulated shot pattern. The comparison shows the extra expected cost of your target against the best sampled target, rather than official strokes gained for a real shot.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: We estimate one stroke + penalties + strokes remaining . Lower is better. We compare direction and depth using a broad grid (6 yd left/right, 10 yd short/long), then refine near its best target in 2 yd steps. Search covers each hole’s aiming range (normally 60 yd left to 60 right; sharp doglegs allow 120 yd each side) within each hole’s depth range, and includes your selected target. Basic targets obey the same distance limit and automatic club model; dispersion changes with club and distance. Member targets use the same saved bag and the same distance-scaling rule. The best sampled target is an approximation, not a proven global optimum.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Quick feedback: “strong decision” means within 0.05 expected strokes of the best sampled target. “Too aggressive” means water, OB, bunker or tree exposure is more than 2 percentage points higher (or all shots are OB). “Too conservative” means the nominal mean is over 5 yd farther from the pin without that extra exposure. Other cases say “target needs refining” so we do not force a misleading label.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Score = max(0, 100 − 60 × extra expected strokes). A score of 100 requires a target within 2 yd of the best sampled target and within 0.005 extra expected strokes. Other nearly equal choices are capped at 99. The comparison is approximate; a 100 is not a guaranteed good shot.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Green front/back yardages are measured along the ball-to-green-center line; flag yardage is the direct distance from the ball. Tap the decision rating after commitment to open a lesson with the actual hazard rates, proximity, club and target adjustment behind the recommendation. Member-preview progress stores the latest 1,000 attempts on this device. Trends use first attempts only, with separate profiles when shot or scoring assumptions change; retries remain separate. Varied hole difficulty means these trends are practice feedback, not a measured real-world skill improvement.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Comparisons use the same 4,000 random draws. Approximate ±95% Monte Carlo error covers sampling noise only, not uncertainty in these assumptions.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: OB: stroke and distance. A shot plus a one-stroke penalty returns you to the original spot; the same strategy is repeated in the expectation calculation.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Water: one penalty stroke plus remaining strokes from a fixed, scenario-specific drop location. This is a simplified relief assumption.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: The animated array shows 48 evenly spaced examples from the 4,000 scored shots. Colors describe their final outcomes; the exact percentages come from all 4,000. Flight arcs and camera motion are illustrations, not a physics model. Dispersion dots use the same outcome colors as the tracers. Your dots are filled; comparison dots are hollow. Solid gold and dashed blue outlines identify the two 80% core contours.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Practice uses fourteen authored hole families with seeded variations, rather than a fixed list to choose from. Par-5 second shots include an open green and a forced water carry, with layup depths available. They appear in Approach and Mixed practice and use the same approach club limits (no driver or rollout). Tee / Approach / Mixed filters control Next shot. Mixed favors the other shot type and avoids recently used families when possible. Next shot varies width, length and safe pin position; doglegs can bend left or right. Geometry moves together so the view and scoring stay aligned. Retry this hole keeps the exact layout and random sample.

entries.section: Model explanation, sources and assumptions
entries.text: Water is checked at carry and during roll. Wooded corridors vary independently on each side in setback, density, start distance and visual height. Dense woods use a higher modeled recovery cost than open woods. These are endpoint recovery zones inside the white stakes; tree height does not affect airborne shots. Vegetation beyond the stakes remains OB. Woodland, Pacific Coast, desert and mountain settings vary the scenery on these layouts. Mountain peaks and evergreen trees are visual only. Lakeside and oceanfront settings appear on layouts with an existing scored side-water hazard; distant water scenery is outside the playable hole. The elevated view places tee shots 9 m and approaches 8 m above their landing areas while retaining a 1.7 m eye height above the ball. Raised greens, sunken bunkers and pond banks add illustrative surface relief, exaggerated for readability. The exposed hazard bowls are a visual teaching aid. Aim points, pins and tracer contacts follow those surfaces while hazard footprints and outcome scoring remain in the same 2D yard coordinates. This is visual terrain only: downhill carry, wind, slope-dependent roll and airborne tree contact are not modeled.
